props.title: The Graduate
props.initialSlug: College grad seduced by older woman, loves daughter

sections.content: The Graduate revolutionized American cinema with its razor-sharp critique of middle-class values and generational alienation. Mike Nichols' masterpiece caught the countercultural zeitgeist through Benjamin Braddock's post-college ennui, creating a template for coming-of-age stories that influenced films like Garden State (2004) and 500 Days of Summer (2009). The film's innovative use of Simon & Garfunkel's music established a new relationship between popular songs and cinema, while Robert Surtees' groundbreaking cinematography - particularly the iconic final bus scene - inspired directors like Wes Anderson and Sofia Coppola.

sections.content: The seduction subplot between Mrs. Robinson and Benjamin influenced countless May-December romance films, from Manhattan (1979) to Notes on a Scandal (2006). But what makes The Graduate endure is its perfect capture of youthful uncertainty. The swimming pool scenes, with Benjamin floating aimlessly in his parents' backyard, became a visual metaphor for post-college drift that films like Reality Bites (1994) and Frances Ha (2012) would later echo.

Dustin Hoffman's breakthrough performance as Benjamin established a new kind of male protagonist - awkward, uncertain, anti-heroic. This marked a dramatic shift from the confident leading men of Classic Hollywood, paving the way for characters in films like Annie Hall (1977) and Rushmore (1998). The film's ambiguous ending, with Benjamin and Elaine sitting stunned on the bus after their dramatic chapel escape, influenced countless subsequent films about the uncertainty of young love. sections.content: The film's critique of suburban emptiness and plastics-driven consumerism resonated deeply with Baby Boomers and continues to influence films about generational disconnect. American Beauty (1999) directly references several Graduate scenes, while Lady Bird (2017) updates its themes of class anxiety and escape for a new generation. The film's innovative use of subjective camera work, particularly in the scuba suit sequence, influenced directors like Martin Scorsese and influenced the language of psychological alienation in cinema.
